utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, as you are aware, the Chamber granted this morning provisional release for Mr. Haradinaj. Have I well understood that Mr. Haradinaj gives his consent that we proceed in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to add to that which the Chamber very much regrets the circumstances which led Mr. Haradinaj to apply for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may I express my personal condolences and those of all Defence teams to the Haradinaj family following the sad death of Mr. Haradinaj's 11-year-old nephew, Shqipton Haradinaj in a road traffic accident yesterday afternoon in Prishtine. And I also express my thanks to the Registry and the Chamber for the manner in which this matter was dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution also expresses its condolences to the family for what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, there was one procedural matter, that is how far the Chamber is in respect of the witness who will testify tomorrow. As I said yesterday, it's a lot of work, and the Chamber, as a matter of fact, gave priority, especially yesterday evening and tomorrow, on other matters, so we are not yet at a point where we could give you any further guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand that the Prosecution propose to file a written response this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- Mr. Re, is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, I will where -- yes, it will be a short written -- written response on the legal aspects which Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Emmerson has raised in his matter. It will be dealing generally with the points raised. It won't be going to specifics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It will only be a few pages long, and we should have it done later. Definitely this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will read it and we'll try to make as much progress as possible, but as I said yesterday, it's quite a lot of work. The comments are -- studying the annexes, it takes certainly some time. And we do not know whether we can fully complete all of the work in full detail by tomorrow in the afternoon. But we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I -- may I make it absolutely clear. We obviously only received the statement and annexes at very close of business, as in 11.00 at night on Wednesday of last week. And that's the reason the matter comes before the Chamber in the way it does and also the reason why we suggest it would be preferable if an alternate witness were found for tomorrow so that sufficient time were set aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We also have raised as a legal matter that particular issue in terms of the delivery of the annexes in the manner in which they come to us, based upon prior rulings of this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey, you join the observations made by other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I do and I have done so in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As we have seen in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness is Professor Lecomte, and Mr. Dutertre will be dealing with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I -- yes, Mr. Dutertre. Then could the usher bring the witness into the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Are you Mrs. Lecomte?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm Professor Lecomte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I'd like to welcome you here. Let me proceed in English. Before you testify, you have to take the solemn declaration provided for by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I'd like you to take the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. [In English] Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Dutertre, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Lecomte, I'm going to ask you to give us your particulars, but before doing so, one observation: Both of us speak French, and therefore I would like to ask you to make sure that the translation of what you or I are saying is -- is completed before -- before answering so as not to have any overlap between the end of the translation of my questions and the beginning of your answers. Is your name Dominique Lecomte? Are you a French national?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: My name is Dominique Lecomte. I am a French national. I am a professor of medicine as the University of Paris, Paris V. I'm the head of the forensic institute in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What is your date of birth and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of March, 1946 in Tignieu-Jameyzieu.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 2072. That's 2072 on the 65 ter list. It's a CV. The document will be displayed on your screen in a few seconds. Professor, is this your CV?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like the witness to be shown 65 ter document 2073, 2073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, are you tendering this CV? Because otherwise we get a lot of documents under one number. We'd then assign a number now and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can assign a number immediately, Your Honour. I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's P926, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any objections? Then it is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I'd like to have document 2073 on the 65 ter list shown to the witness now. Professor, the document is now on your screen. Is this the CV of your colleague, Dr. Walter Vorhauer?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P927.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections? Then P927 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like the witness to be shown 65 ter document 2071. 2071.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, do you recognise this document? Is this the first expert report you prepared in relation to the forensic operations conducted at the Lake Radonjic canal in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to have page 31 of the report displayed in Sanction. Page 31. And please zoom in on the upper part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: A number of questions were put to you, and they read as -- read as follows, the first one being: Provide an opinion on how bodies were recovered, recorded, transported, preserved, autopsied, and identified, and on the 'traceability' of the said bodies." And your answer to this question was, and I quote: "The matches between the photographs of the discovered bodies and the photographs of the autopsy operations enable an evaluation of traceability. We are told that the bodies were transported under a protective 'patrol' up to the Hotel Pastrik in Djakovica. The autopsies were performed in appropriate conditions, considering the environmental context." I'd like to put a number of questions to you with respect to this answer of yours. Could you please tell us a bit more about the traceability of the bodies between the crime scene and the location where the autopsies were conducted at the Pastrik Hotel. Could you please give us some more details about this.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: We worked on the basis of photographs and reports. The reports -- the photographs taken where the bodies were recovered were photographs of the bodies as where they were found on site. But for some of the bodies, we had photographs of bodies in the body bags, before they had been transported, and this caused a problem to us because the number was not affixed to each body. It was on a loose tag. However, the number given was the same as the number we found on the -- in the autopsy reports. And when we had the photographs of the body in the body bag, when the bodies were collected, the bodies looked like the bodies we saw photographed on the autopsy tables. In other words, we had no difficulty regarding traceability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll read the third sentence: "The autopsies were performed in appropriate conditions, considering the environmental context"? With respect to this sentence, can you give us some more detail, especially when you talk about the environmental context.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: The word I used, "environmental context," was a very broad term, or "environmental difficulties," was a very broad term that my colleagues may have been confronted with on the site where they recovered the bodies. Their work - and I mention it in this first report - the work, the forensic work conducted on the bodies in the institute, in the morgue and later on in Belgrade, this work was conducted very meticulously. This work was conducted by forensic physicians who, like all forensic physicians in the world, are very accurate observers of the things. Therefore, the examination of the bodies conducted at a distance where the bodies were recovered was done very meticulously. But as for the work conducted at the place where the bodies were recovered, we were faced with a number of difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Let me just first focus on the autopsies themselves. Sorry for interrupting you. You mentioned an institute. Are you referring to the Hotel Pastrik, where the autopsies were conducted?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. I would now like page 30 to be displayed with Sanction, and I'm interested in the second paragraph on that particular page. And I quote: "The causes of death were given in the report's conclusions, however the ambiguity therein is regrettable. In fact, the report often states that the cause of death cannot be determined, when in fact gunshot wounds and bone traumatisms are clearly identifiable." And I have the following question for you, Professor: Could you please be more specific and tell us why -- what caused this ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: When we worked on the basis of the autopsy reports conducted by the Serbian forensic physicians, we realised that their work had been done very meticulously. I've said it before. They gave very good explanations about gunshot wounds, about various trauma. And the photographs we had at our disposals pictured the gunshot wounds and various trauma. However, when it comes to their conclusions about the cause of death, very often the reports read that the cause of death could not be determined. That's why we use the word "ambiguity" in our own report, because in my opinion, when you have traumatic lesions, when you have gunshot wounds and when the person in question is dead, then obviously there is a link you should not ignore. Therefore, to say that there's no cause of death whether you have gunshot wounds in the skull with bullets going through the skull, we -- both of us found that slightly ambiguous. I'm talking about their answer, their conclusion about the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When you talk about you, when you say "we," you mean yourself and your colleague, Dr. Vorhauer?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Could you give us the reasons for this ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: When you work as forensic physicians on dead bodies with gunshot wounds in the cranium, obviously the death has been caused by the gunshot wound to the skull. Therefore saying that the cause of death cannot be determined in such a case is ambiguous indeed, because we would expect the cause of death to be specified and you would not expect the report to include the fact that the cause of death cannot be determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you believe that they erred on the side of caution?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I would not dare to make any comment about this, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the first report of Ms. Lecomte.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's P928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Therefore, P928 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. The OTP had notified the Chamber that we did not want to use the second report for reasons we explained earlier on, but it is notably because we believe that entomological criteria and parameters were not used in the appropriate manner, therefore I have now completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That may give rise to some logistical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because I've been endeavouring to ascertain from the Prosecution over the last two days how it was they proposed to deal with the second report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm afraid I wasn't able to get an answer at all. And indeed I repeated my question just before the Tribunal sat this afternoon and still didn't get an answer. Now, I don't know whether Professor Lecomte has a hard copy of her second report available to her in the witness box. I wonder whether she might be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a -- a copy of your second report, a hard copy available to you at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I cannot see whether it's -- it's a clean copy or whether you made any markings in it, whether you made any comments in it. That might be of importance perhaps for the Defence to know in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To assist the Chamber, let me say that we have a clean copy of the report here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam le Professor, do you have a clean copy in front of you or an annotated copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are annotations on this report, because as I was on the train earlier on today, I wrote a number of things of my -- on my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest that you keep it nearby. If you want to consult any annotations, that you indicate and ask my permission to do so, but that we start working on the basis of a clean copy. Mr. Dutertre, if you would provide Madam le Professor avec un clean copy of her report, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can I indicate that the -- the report is in e-court. It is 65 ter 1986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have no access to all the uploaded documents in e-court automatically, but I think that we have somewhere else on our computers a copy. Let me just check whether I get ... Let me find it for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see it's coming up on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte, may I ask you, first of all, some questions about your background experience in dealing with multiple body scenes in the former Yugoslavia. Have you conducted crime scene investigations on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor in the past in various parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was head of a mission to -- as a forensic specialist to examine bodies that had been recovered next to Mitrovica in the area controlled by France. These were bodies of people who had been buried in the ground. I conducted more than 400 exhumations in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I'm going now to ask you some questions about the document which appears on your screen, but should, I hope, be the first document in your file as well, which is the letter of instruction you received from the Office of the Prosecutor on -- dated the 23rd of April, 2007, asking you to prepare a second report. Were you informed then in that letter that the Defence for Mr. Haradinaj had raised issues in the pre-trial brief and in cross-examination concerning the integrity, that is, the authenticity of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of this. When I received this document, I worked without any prior information on anything. I worked only as a forensic physician. I analysed photographs, reports, et cetera. But I was not informed about anything else. And in any case, I would not have wished to be informed of such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm -- I think it may be that my question was insufficiently clear. In this letter that was sent to you on the 23rd of April, the Prosecution, we can see, informed you that the Defence had raised questions about the possible movement of bodies, and you were being asked to give observations on the authenticity of the crime scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes. But you see, this is a comment among others in this letter. Yes, I see that. Paramilitaries are mentioned here. But this is not the purpose of my work, the object of my work. I always work on the basis of the questions that are being asked to me. I always worked on the basis -- work on the basis of the documents I'm asked to analyse. If somebody raises an issue, I have no idea whether it's valid or not, that challenge. For me it has no bearing on the quality of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I entirely understand that. And like all scientists, you need to be provided with specific questions so that you can give specific answers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in this instance, you were asked in respect of each body to estimate, first of all, the date of death; that is, how long the body had been dead. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then secondly, taking account of the material in your possession, your estimate of the period of time that it had been at the discovery site; correct? Questions are listed in the letter at the front of the file.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes. And I gave a response for each body examined in my report with respect to questions 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If we can just go through them so that we're clear. Question 3, then, asked you to record any other forensic medical conclusions that might be relevant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And question 4 specifically asked you to submit any other comments that might be useful for determination of the authenticity of the crime scenes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading the question, and usually this is -- and this is part of the discussion and the concluding part of our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that is what you sought to do in respect of each of the bodies that you examined.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you've listed in your report all of the materials you had available to you, the videos, the photographs of the remains in situ, the photographs of the autopsy process and all of the autopsy reports. Yes?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, I just want to see if you can help us, please, first of all with some terminology, some of the terminology you've used in your report. When answering the second question for each body, that is, the period of time that it had been at the discovery site, you have divided the bodies according to the locations where they are recorded as having been found. And I want to concentrate, first of all, please, on the group of remains that are recorded as having been found on the ground adjacent to the concrete canal wall. That would be bodies R1 through to R17. Now, in respect of each of those sets of remains, you have given an estimation of how long the set of remains had been in the position in which it is recorded as having been found. And you summarise your conclusions in that regard on page 114 in a table. That's 114 of the French version, of the original version of the report, and page 53 in the English translation. And we can see, if we look at that table, that you record in the centre column the length of time in your estimation the person concerned had been dead. And in the right-hand column, the length of time that in your opinion the remains had been present at the scene where they were found. And we can see in the right-hand column that in all but three cases you use the expression "very short time," and in three of the cases you use the expression "short time." I want you to help us, please, if you can, first of all, as to what the distinction between a short time and a very short time is, in terms of days. When you use the expression "very short time," what are we to understand by that as distinct from "short time"?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: If I did not include a number of days, it's because a physician is not a clairvoyant. A forensic physician only makes notices, notices something, and then includes or writes what I wrote. It is very difficult to say three days and how many minutes. When I say that it's a short stay, I would say that -- a short time, that it's something less than eight days. I don't know if it's six or seven. And when I talk about a very short time, I am thinking of less than eight days. But it can be four days, five days, two days. And when I say that the body may have stayed there for a short time, that's even shorter; meaning, a few days, two days or three days or going up to four days. But let's say that the appreciation is something that's very subjective, and I hope that you will understand this, and it has to deal with the experience that we have, my colleague and myself, in order to see and in order to examine the bodies. We have the pictures, we had the environment. They talked to us about bad weather, for instance that, had taken place. So by taking all these elements into account - and please allow me to finish - the work -- this type of work was done for each of the bodies. And this table is only a collated result.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt you, Professor Lecomte. I'm going to go back in more detail in respect to some of the remains in due course. At the moment, I'm just concentrating on what the language means. Now, it may be that there was a problem with translation in the answers that you've just given. I don't know. But you have said on the transcript that where you use the expression "short time," you mean less than eight days but where -- I'm sorry. Let me just be absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness said eight days or less or it could be six or seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to be absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is purely a matter of terminology. I just want to understand what you mean by these expressions. Is it correct that when you say a "very short time," you mean a matter of three, four, or five days; and when you say a "short time," you mean less than eight days? Is that how I am to understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness already answered that question when she answered the first question. It seemed very clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It -- there may be a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because it seemed to me to be the natural inverse of what the witness was seeking to say. So perhaps we can just clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte, just so that we're clear, you've used two different expressions here. You've used a "short time" for some of the bodies and a "very short time" for the other bodies. And presumably when you say a "very short time" you mean less than the period of time applicable to those bodies for whom you say a "short time"? We --

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We understand that this is not a precise science. But when you say a "short time -- when you say a "short time," which you do, for example, here for R-16, R-17, and R-7, have I understood correctly, when you say a "short time," you mean something in the region of about eight days or less? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: If I may, I know that I may be unpleasant now, but I have to say that a forensic physician is not a clairvoyant. We have to work on each of the bodies. And there are various elements that enable us to say what we conclude. Rather than saying something rather general and -- something rather general that will not perhaps clearly state what the report is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm just at this stage trying to clarify the terms, Professor Lecomte. So you mentioned periods of eight days and periods of three days. Can I summarise it with you in this way: That for each of these sets of remains that appear in the table on page 114, for each of them you considered that their -- they had been present at the location for no more than about eight days; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No, I cannot allow myself as a forensic physician to say that it's no more than eight days. It could be nine days. It can be ten days. But I cannot say anything else. I cannot assess and give you a figure when you have a photograph of a body that is shown on a picture during the recovery -- recovery operation. If I may say so, the recovery operation was badly done. The photographs are not clear enough, not relevant enough in order to tell us to say how many days they were there. We just examined or looked at the bodies where they were photographed at -- for instance, at the autopsy room, we had a better visibility of the bodies. But I maintain that in my mind a "short time" and "very short time" is not something that we should dwell too much upon. It would not reflect -- it would not be necessarily -- particularly important for this report. When we say "short stay," it could be eight days, six days, seven day. But when it's very short time, it's shorter than short time but it can also be seven days. It could also go up to eight days. But I do not want to insist on this eight days that you are mentioning, because eight days is not something that a competent forensic physician can say. We do not have this type of precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I -- I entirely understand that, Professor Lecomte, and I'm not seeking to pin you down to a specific number of days at all. And I entirely understand that there's a margin of error. What we -- what we're trying to assess from your testimony is whether we're talking about days, weeks, or months. And as -- from what you've told us, your opinion is that these bodies, all of them in that table from R-1 through to R-17, had been for -- you say it could be eight days, nine days, ten days. A matter of days. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: That is correct. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking in terms of days here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So if we could just look at an outer limit, would the outer limit be somewhere like two to three weeks?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I will not answer this question, sir, because I believe that we're not talking in terms of months. In months, we can say something else. But even if you look at the assessment of the bodies just in order to put the date of death, we used months there, and we say -- we used the same terminology, more than one, over one month, less than two months. We cannot, once again, have the precision of a train controller. That is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Absolutely understood. But from what you're telling us, when estimating the period of time that that group of bodies had been in the position in which they are found, that is something that you would estimate in days; whereas, when estimating the length of time that the person has been dead, you are estimating that in multiples of months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness already answered that question. This question was already put to her in various ways. And once again, one is insisting on the duration of the -- from the moment when the person has deceased and the duration of time during which the body was on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether we make much progress at this moment in this respect. Madam Lecomte, what Mr. Emmerson is trying to find out is what you mean by your words. If you use the same words, then one would expect that that word is used for the same range, even if that range is not very precisely defined. And Mr. Emmerson, the only thing he'd like to know, as far as I understand, is if you're talking about a very short time, what approximately that range would be, accepting that for everybody you might perhaps be a bit more to the left of the range or a bit more to the right in that range, but that's the only thing he's trying to find out. And it seems there is a debate ongoing rather than that we have a very clear answer. I'm not saying a very precise answer but a very clear answer to the question. That is, would a very short period of time be anything between two and ten days or one and fifteen days or -- approximately? Because you use a certain term, so therefore if you do not further -- give further precision, that we'd like to know what this range approximately is, where we do understand that the beginning and the end of the range, if it is in days, might cover two or three days. That means four to eighteen days could be two, three, four, five, or six at the lower end and perhaps sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty at the higher end. But that's what Mr. Emmerson is trying to find out. Could you further assist him on these terms about "very short," and "short".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To answer your question, Your Honour, when we put "short time," we're -- and "very short time," we're thinking in terms of days. We're not thinking in terms of months. But in order to get a week, you need eight days. So when we say "very short time," this is an assessment which, according to us, means that we are thinking in days. It's less days of -- less days of -- of presence on site. But we are not working in terms of months and -- or weeks. We work with days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will make a distinction between "very short," and "short." Could you explain what -- where you would say "short," where you would say "very short," because you categorise them as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It all depends, of course, because of the state of body and where the body was recovered. It also depends on other issues; for instance, the body covered with earth or the state of the terrain. It -- it depends on various criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you allow me to interrupt you there for a second. I'm asking what the two categories are. Your answer is explaining to us what the circumstances are which may lead you to categorise one body in the category "short" and the other body in the category "very short." That was not my question. I do understand that you take into consideration all these circumstances, but when would you call it "short"? When would you call it "very short"? You said, "It's short as in days, not month." Now, "very short," would that be within the range of anything between one and ten days or would that also be a category that could cover one to twenty days? Because you're -- you are using different terms, and we're just trying to understand exactly what you mean by that on the basis of all findings and all circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the elements that were examined in order to give this assessment -- and once again, this is an assessment which has to take into account a whole range of elements. But when we talk about a "short time" on site, some bodies were there for a short time and other bodies were there for a very short time, depending on, for instance, if there were larva, if there was the presence of diptera larva, or, for instance, we can notice that clothes is present and that it's still intact. So this is an assessment which is not vague. I'm not saying that this is a vague assessment. But this assessment depends on many criteria. We looked at the photographs. Some pictures we looked with a magnifying glass in order to see if, for instance, there is the presence of humidity or not, if they were buried in a humid soil or not. So all these elements enter into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you again. You're doing exactly the same as I said before you did it; that is, to explain how you come to an assessment. What -- we are seeking something quite different. What we are seeking is that -- I take it that all circumstances taken into consideration -- let's just take an example: That you come to the conclusion that the body has been there for a -- a time, anything between 10 and 23 days. Now, what we would like to know is whether would -- you would then categorise that body as being there for a short time or being there for a very short time. We are trying to understand the different categories you are using yourself, not on how you came to the conclusions in respect of one individual bodily remain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you take, for instance, the two bodies R-16 and R-17. For each it is indicated "short time." Those bodies were buried in the ground. They were covered with earth. So if you will, the assessment is more difficult. So we put these two bodies in a category of "short time," because we did not have sufficient elements. The bodies were covered by earth. That's why we've put "short time." We had less elements to assess. When the bodies are under the earth, when they are buried, it's a different evaluation, it's a different assessment. I'm terribly sorry we are spending so much time with this terminology. It's -- it's -- we should have put "short time" everywhere instead of "very short time." The reason why we put "very," it's because we had elements to believe that it's a very short time; whereas, for the other bodies, R-16 and R-17, those bodies were covered -- covered in earth and they're against a wall, so we don't have enough elements to say how long they were there. So that's why we put "short time." So I would like to insist on the fact that this assessment is not an assessment made without being very precise. It's where the bodies were found. R-16 and R-17 were covered with body [as interpreted]. They were not near the surface, so we cannot really evaluate. We cannot assess. That's why we say these two bodies belong to the category of "short time." Whereas, when you have people who were buried under the earth or accessible or visible, then you can say it's a very short time, because then we have elements that enable us to assess the duration of time. And I have to tell you that this assessment of time is done by taking various criteria into account. We cannot say 10 days, 15 days more or less. It's criteria that enter into account, where the bodies were found and other criteria, of course, especially the aspect of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Emmerson, I suggest you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I just approach that in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we look back at your table, please, on page 114. If you could just turn that table up for a moment. Let me ask you: Do you have the table on page 114? Now, if we just look at the bottom body on that list, R-15. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, we -- we can see that your assessment there is that that person had been dead for a period greater than three months. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the -- the time that the body, in your assessment, had been at the scene is recorded as being a "very short time"; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It's what's written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, from the answers you've already given, a very short time could not include a period greater than three months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No, I did not say that at all, sir. I did not say that a "very short stay" means three months. I said that a "short time" or a "very short time" is determined in days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps there's a translation error.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think there's a translation problem generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll -- from now on I'll listen to the French.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One ear to the French and another --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the question put to you by Mr. Emmerson was that if a body is reported to have been dead for more than three months, that a "very short time" the body was at the location where it was found could not cover more than three months. And Mr. Emmerson, I think, said this on the basis of your previous answer that "very short" would mean in terms of days, rather than of month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe - and I will try to explain everything to you by looking at this table. This is a summary of all of our observations. In this table, the date of death -- the forensic evaluation to have date of death, meaning that a person died on a certain date and that person is discovered. The body is discovered. So with respect to this discovery, without taking into account the environment, we can say that the death occurred over a three-month or -- three months before the death. Why? Because body 15, for instance, is a skeleton, almost completely a total skeleton, with disjointed bones and the internal organs are no longer inside the body, and there's -- there are almost no soft tissues around the bones. There's only skeleton. And so this is a body that is certainly there for more than three months. We can talk about a period that goes over three months. It could be three months, four months, four months and a few days. We're looking at the aspect of the body, the way the body looks through the documents that were given to us and the documents that talk about the autopsy report handed to us by our colleagues. Now, if we take this other body, which is against -- against a wall, and it -- there are little rocks that are at that level, little pebbles. This body did not show the presence of larva. And if I talked about larva or diptera, it's because my colleague, like any other forensic physician, they make a complete observation of the body. They examine the body, they examine the clothes to see if there are larva or not. And when there is a presence of larva, they say that it is an observation. This is what we do in forensic medicine. So my colleagues did not put here "presence of larva" or "diptera." Diptera is something that appears approximately after ten days. From eight to ten days you have the pupa and sometimes even up to twelve days. So there were none. So we're talking about the days in terms of discovery, the discovery of the body. Because these bodies were in fact in a -- on soil. There are little rocks. And there's air going through. It's not a cement prison around them. There is air. Flies can also go through these spaces. So they will lay their eggs. Between the egg and the larva, there's approximately seven days. So we did not see any pupa of diptera, no larva, no vegetation, because it is true that we attached a great importance to the vegetation, because in Kosovo when we worked, vegetation was very important for us. The vegetation enabled us to date, to know when those bodies were buried approximately, because this vegetation takes approximately 20 days to grow back. So it takes 20 days for a plant to resurface or to appear. So here there was no vegetation. You will tell me there were little pebbles. Because of pebbles, that's not very easy for vegetation to grow. But vegetation was vegetation with huge leaves. So there were -- there was vegetation with very large leaves but -- around in the area, but there were some pebbles but there were no leaves around this body so no vegetation. So this is what enabled us to say, once again, we are not a clairvoyant. For us it means that this body has been there for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I, Professor Lecomte, can I ask you, please, just to take this in smaller chunks, because you give us a lot of information in one time and it's quite important for us to understand step by step how you reach the conclusions that you do. Now, I just -- please just wait for the question and then concentrate on -- on, if you can, specifically the information that I'm looking for. If we look back at your table on page 114. I was asking you questions about body R-15, and you've told us already that in your assessment that body had been dead for more than three months but its presence at the scene was for a very short time, which you say is a matter of days. And what I want to understand from that is -- just to use body R-15 as an example: The implication of your finding seems to be that this body had been dead in some other location at an earlier time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: If you look at my report, if you read my report, you will see that in the end, in the conclusion, it says -- and I would like to give you the exact terminology. It says that these bodies can very well have been buried somewhere; meaning they were buried somewhere. Somebody dug a hole. They put the body there. It's a hermetical hole. And then at page 119 of my report, they were transported on site. I am saying that nothing enables us to eliminate an initial burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: A primary burial. But I am terribly sorry to be giving you so many -- so much information, but you're answering me to answer to questions which are complex. I have to work on many factors of your question in order to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's -- that's understood. But just to -- just to be absolutely clear, in respect of body R-15, if it has been dead for more than three months but in your opinion has been at the scene for only a matter of days, that suggests, does it not, that the body was dead in some different location at an earlier time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: You are indeed correct, sir. And if you take a look at page 119 of my report, you will see that this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: "Nothing can preclude there being a primary burial."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. I entirely understand. And if we can now just look at the others. That -- that presumably applies as well, then, if we just look down the list, to the other bodies that are listed as having been dead for more than three months; that is, on your table: R-3, R-5, R-7, R-8, R-10, and R-15. Presumably the same conclusion follows in respect of those.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I will have to take these cases, because I tell you that I am basing my conclusions on several criteria. If we take all of these cases, we can see ... If you don't mind. I apologise. I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte, can I assist you to this extent. I'm going to take you in a little while to some specific examples. So at the moment, I'm just understanding the -- the import of your evidence. Now, you've told us with R-15 because it was dead more than three months and, in your opinion, had only been at the scene for a few days, the implication is that it must have been or was likely to have been dead in some other location beforehand. And all I'm asking you at this stage is: That presumably -- that same conclusion would apply to each body which, in your opinion, had been dead for more than three months but which had been at the scene for only a very short time. The same conclusion would follow.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it -- does it also apply to those bodies for whom you have recorded an opinion that they had been dead for two months or more? But had only been at the scene for a matter of days? Is the same conclusion applicable in the case of bodies dead for two months or more?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I'll give you the same answer, sir. I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then -- and then finally, is it also correct for those bodies that are recorded in your opinion to have been dead for more than one month?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I think so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think -- yes. Sorry. I will take my questions today -- the reason I'm asking you to deal with them in small chunks is because we are speaking through an interpreter, and I think it's possible that some of the nuances of the questions and answers get lost in translation. So it is -- it is much easier if we simply take it in -- in short chunks and then we'll get the information clear. Now, if -- if we look through the -- the body of the report where you go through each of these sets of remains one by one, we can see that for that group of bodies that are recorded as being found by the side of the canal, that is, R-1 through to R-17, you very often record the opinion that the body has been previously buried. So that is the position with R-1, R-2, R-3, R-4, R-5, R-7, R-8, R-9, R-10, R-12, R-13, R-14. Those particular sets of remains. In each instance, you have -- you have recorded, in answer to question number 3, "the totality indicates prior burial." Now, I just want to understand. When you say "prior burial," do you mean burial at some other location to the location at which they were found? Is that what "prior burial" means?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Of course. "Burial," that means placing in the earth, once the earth has been dug, so that it is then hermetically sealed. When a body is buried in the earth, it's either in a coffin that is closed or in the -- at the base of the dug part of the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But just -- just to be clear, just to be absolutely clear, the emphasis I am placing is on the word "prior." When you say "prior burial," do you mean burial at some previous location to the location in which the body is recorded as having been found in the material that you were shown from the Serbian operation?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was very clear in the report, because I say that the estimated date of death is above three months and I say a short stay at the place. That means obviously that the body has been buried elsewhere. And I say there's no presence of flies because there has been this burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's -- I'm just making sure that it's -- that I have understood what it is that your report is concluding. Now, with a number of the bodies, you also record -- and I'm only looking at conclusions at the moment. We'll look at the reasons in -- in a moment or two. But with a number of the bodies -- and I'm going to indicate in particular R-3, R-5, R-8, and R-10 -- you also record an opinion that in addition to prior burial, one factor or another has led you to conclude that the remains have been handled. You say, for example, in relation to R-3, "the totality indicates prior burial and the entanglement of the bones indicates handling." And in the case of R-5, you say "the totality indicates prior burial, while the separation of the bones indicates handling." Now, it's the handling I want to ask you about. Do you mean handling of the body before it found its place in the position where it is recorded as having been found by the Serbian team?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No. For instance, for R-3 that you referred to, we have an indication of a prior burial shortly after death, in other words, the body was buried, buried in a deep grave. And the entanglement of the bones indicates handling. Now, I think if the body was transported given the state of putrefaction, if we're talking about three months later on. And looking at this, if we have bones, bones are no longer retained by the soft tissue and when the body is transported to another site, there is a tendency for the bones to become entangled. If you leave a body in situ and if the person died at that position, then there'll be no movement. There'll be no change as regards the initial position of the body. It will be in the same position it was when the person died and was buried. There will be no movement of the body unless somebody actually moves it. And here we have an entanglement of bones, which means that that body, in all likelihood - and that's why I say "indicates" - in all likelihood has been transported and handled, because otherwise you die, you're in your coffin, you're lying on your back, and you won't be discovered sometime down the road as a pile of bones. That will only happen if the coffin has moved or been moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I -- I think that is exactly what I was seeking to clarify. The handling you're referring to there is handling of the body between the time when it was first buried somewhere else and the time when it was found adjacent to the canal wall, some handling between those two points in time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could then look at R-13 for a moment. You use a slightly different expression there. I just want to know whether that means something different or the same. With R-13, you say: "The totality indicates that the body was transported after prior burial in the ground." Does "transported" mean anything different from "handled" or is it the same concept that we are to understand?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It is indeed the same concept. Transporting, handling, carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Whatever. It's the same concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And just for the sake of -- just for the sake of clarity, at -- in the case of R-14, you say: "The totality indicates prior burial and movement of the skeleton." That again, do I understand it correctly, is the same concept? Movement of the skeleton between prior burial and the place where it was found?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in respect of these sets of remains, to take in as a whole R-1 to R-17, do I understand your conclusion to be that the appearance of this group of bodies led you to conclude that it was more likely than not that they had been moved after previously being buried somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So what I want to do now is just to look in a little bit more detail with you at the criteria that you examined. And I think you are aware, because Mr. Dutertre has communicated to you for the Prosecution, some evidence of Mr. Dourel on the entomological aspects of this. I want to look at all of the factors with you, please that led you to reach the conclusions that you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I see the time. I don't know whether before I embark on Your Honour would think this the appropriate moment to take a break. I'm happy to carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for very technical reasons we can't go on, because we have our -- we are running out of tapes. Our interpreters need some rest as well. Therefore, I think we'd have a break now until five minutes past 4.00. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Could we have some broad idea of the time required for cross-examination? Given the questions being put, I will also need a certain amount of time, perhaps a considerable amount of time for redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm -- given that I'm, in effect, in the position of having to elicit from this witness the evidence in chief in relation to these matters, I -- I would have thought at least another hour and a half, possibly a little longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And after that, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, considering the state that we're in where we are, as Mr. Emmerson said, dealing with the report of the professor which was sought by the Prosecution, I think that I probably will have very little cross -- cross-examination or examination at all, because the matters will be covered in an attempt to bring the information that the Chamber needs to light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I shall not have anything to add to the questions that Mr. Emmerson asks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Emmerson, the second report of Professor Lecomte, would you like to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will -- I certainly wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll ask a number to be assigned to that. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's D166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any objections, Mr. Dutertre? Then D166 is already admitted into evidence, although the examination of the witness has not been concluded yet. We'll have a break until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte, I want now, if I may, just to go through with you in a little bit more detail some of the criteria that you used in order to reach your overall evaluations about the date of death and the length of presence at the scene. But before I do that, I want to put aside for a moment the question of the presence or absence of larvae. That's something I'm going to come back to. I want to look, first of all, at some of the other criteria that you list in your report as being relevant and just ask, if you would, just very briefly one by one to insist the Trial Chamber in understanding the relevance of those criteria. Now, first of all, you said, I think, in answer to a question before the break that -- that amongst the factors that you took into consideration was information that you had about the weather and the environmental conditions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I knew that between the day when the bodies were discovered and the day when they returned to the site that there was a violent storm. I believe that this was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And amongst the factors that you list as relevant, if we could just go through them briefly -- are the following: First of all, missing bones or parts of the skeleton. Is that a -- a relevant factor in determining the question of how long the body had been at the scene?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't. The fact that there were bones that were missing -- for instance, in the case of R-13 that we were talking about earlier on, there were bones missing that have not been found at the site. So that is somewhat awkward. Where are those bones? Which in fact led us to raise the next question. All of this would imply that the body was transported after prior burial in the ground because during the transport or the collection, shall we say, of the body that was initially -- or previously buried, there might have been a bone that went missing. You have to understand that this body after all was over three months old, so obviously it -- its appearance and its state had been affected. Perhaps it was two months. But anyhow, there was a missing bone. But the fact that you have missing bonings in many cases is an element that led us to say -- that enabled us to say that some sort of transport had occurred, because we didn't recover those bones in situ.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And similarly, we can see in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could I ask one clarifying question here. It might save time at a later stage. You said missing bones in many cases is an element that led you -- that enabled you "to say that some sort of transport had occurred, because we didn't recover those bones in situ." I -- I'm trying to understand your answer. Are you saying that the body was transferred -- transported to that place where bones may have been lost during transportation, or is it also a possibility that the bones, the missing bones, were taken from the spot where the body was and always had been and then removed to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Perhaps I'm not stating it very clearly. What I'm trying to say - and I'm trying to explain that this criterion -- actually, it's rather, an element, not so much a criterion - but this was something that was noted by my colleagues who produced the autopsies report. They said they noted that there were bones that were missing from the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall exactly what it was in this case, but, for instance, you had a forearm, a bone that was missing, part of the foot bone was missing or one of the bones. So at the site where the remains were found, that forearm and that part of the foot was not found. And the question is: Why were they not present? And we evoked the fact -- we mentioned the fact that they probably came from somewhere else, and when they were picked up from this other point - for example, they'd been taken out of the earth - and the whole body didn't come because it had already suffered the consequences of putrefaction; in other words, the body wasn't entire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your answer. But what makes that more probable -- let's say we have a -- I don't know how many bones there are in the body but let's just for argument's sake say there are 100 bones. Now, you find 95. Isn't it true that the 95 bones you found could have been brought there and the remaining, the other five, were left somewhere else, or that the body with all the 100 bones had always been at that place but 5 bones were taken away by animals, by persons, by whomever and taken to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Let me put it this way: I think we have to be reasonable in stating the facts. When I die, my body will be in a certain position with all of its bones in place. Gradually the muscle mass will disappear and the bones will separate. But I will still be in the position that you put me in when I was buried in the ground or in a coffin. If you find me at the base of a wall, at the foot of a wall dislocated - in other words, without any muscle, without the soft tissue, with just the bones and you find that there's the forearm or a femur or part of the foot that's missing - then obviously this begs questions, if you find that there are several bodies in this state. So you can assume perhaps that I have been transported from the place where I was originally. I've been picked up or my -- I don't know, My coffin has been thrown into something or the bodies have been dug up and taken off somewhere else. And the bones missing probably remained at the original site. For example, when the body was taken out of the ground. The case of the predator is somewhat different. A predator is an animal -- I mean, we know that in Kosovo there have been many -- there were many predators. I mean, I have been there. I was there in September. And there were many dogs, wild dogs who are very hungry, you know, looking for food to eat. And it's true that those dogs can attack bodies. And in the examination we had one body such as this that had very clearly been attacked. The fragment of the body was not very far removed from the body but had been torn to pieces. So there we assume that there was probably a predator. The predators don't take the bones and travel kilometres. The predators are generally dogs. And what they do, they get their teeth round the muscle. They pull it from side to side to try and tear it off the bone. But they aren't terribly interested in the bones, so the bone will be thrown out by the -- from the dog's mouth by it shaking its head. But it's not going to be kilometres away; it will be close to the site. So I eliminate the possibility of there being predators for most of these cases. And there have even been cases - and I think you've probably seen this in reading the report - where there was clothing but no body. And there were other cases where there was a bone that didn't correspond to the body. This has been noted by my colleagues. And all of this gives us the impression that there's been some movement, that something has happened before the discovery of the bodies and the remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you note as one of the criteria in relation to each body whether or not there are predator lesions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, for example, with body R-4 -- body R-4, you have recorded the presence of predator lesions where they are to be found; is that right? If you look at the conclusions: "In relation to body R-4," question number 3, you've recorded there where predator lesions are evident. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I can indeed confirm this. I also have the photograph in front of me, and we can see that it's been torn and it is close to the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And so we -- can we assume therefore that with each of these bodies where there were missing bones, you were looking to see whether there was evidence of predator lesions or not?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. When we take a look at the bones and the photos taken by my colleagues at the -- on the autopsy table, we could see very clearly that there are bones that are missing, the bones are quite clearly not there. Let's take other examples of this, if you like. R-5, for instance. On the photo, the lower part of the legs is missing. It's the left leg, in fact. The right femur is missing. These are important bones. And, in fact, in the conclusion I said: "The totality indicates that there's been handling because of separation of the bones," and somewhere or other I've put: "Where are the missing bones?" So a forensic scientist inevitably asks this question when he or she has examined the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we just look back at R-4 for a moment, because you've noted that R-4 was found lying on the surface and in the open air. Now, this is your paragraph 2 under the -- under the body R-4. You've said: "Lying on the surface in the open air and appears to have been placed on the ground, mangled at the trunk." Now, mangled at the trunk. Just so that I understand, entanglement of bones is a factor that you have recorded in a number of instances as relevant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Well, this is a different case. It's not a tangling of bones. It's not a mix-up of bones. This is the trunk, the body in itself, in other words, that has been torn or mangled. I mean, there are parts of the flesh that have been torn away from the body which indicates the presence of a predator. And the body was indeed on the surface of the earth. And I would like to say - and this is very important - this body was not terribly old. It was one or two months old. There was still soft tissue present.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we can see under question number 3 that despite being found on the surface, the clothing of that body was filled with soil; that is, presumably soil on the inside of the clothes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Well, I worked on the basis of my colleagues' reports. When it says "filled with earth," that means that there is soil stuck to the clothing. I think that the state of putrefaction was significant in this body. In fact, it says "chewed by predators," if we're taking a look at what my colleagues have written for R-4. Yes, "Advanced state of putrefaction." But when a body is deceased -- when there is water in the body, which means that there are liquids that are going to leave the body, and these humours, this putrid liquid will be between the body and the clothing and the clothing will be slightly damp and may indeed become covered by soil, if there is soil at that particular location. And there was -- there were also diptera larvae as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll come back to larvae in a minute. Another factor that you describe in the report as being -- or you list in the report is the presence or absence of desiccation. Could you just help us as to what "desiccation" means in this context.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: When a body is deceased, the skin, the envelope, which is what our skin is, is in contact with the air. And if we're in a well-aired place, the body will dehydrate. It will lose its water. It will lose its elasticity. It will dry out, become desiccated. So over time we can end up with mummification, a sort of parchment aspect. The skin has lost its water, its humidity and looks like a card or parchment. So desiccation is something that takes place over a certain length of time, say 48 hours. You have to be in the open air. 48 hours or three days. I mean, it depends on all of the other factors as well, ambient humidity and so on. But you will see that the skin will be desiccated. And so we can say -- it's one of the criteria. We can say that when there's no desiccated skin, then that body has not been in the open air just after death.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Another criteria you list in relation to a number of the sets of remains is the absence of penetration by roots or grass. Can you just explain to us what you would expect to find if a body had been in situ for, let us say, several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No roots are mentioned in the report, Your Honour. It might be a mistake by Mr. Emmerson. Branches are mentioned, but no roots are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's -- I'm sorry. You're quite right. It's branches, rather than roots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But -- but let me put the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: More generically.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In a number of instances, you mention the absence of colonisation by vegetation, grass, branches. Can you just help the Tribunal understand why that is relevant to determining the length of time that the remains may have been at the scene.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: When a body is placed on the ground with grass or when the earth has been moved, you have a body lying on the ground. And if there is vegetation around the body, if the body is located where there is grass growing, this grass is going to grow back around the body, because the body is going to lose putrid matters that will help the vegetation grow back around it; therefore, the body will be surrounded, even sometimes covered by vegetation and you will often find bodies in the fields or in the undergrowth that are covered by the grass. The grass grows back above the body sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with each of your conclusions for each body, when you are expressing a view on the length of time it has been present at the location and when you are expressing a view on whether or not it had been moved or previously buried, you use the word "totality," the totality indicates prior burial or the totality indicates a short presence. And I think you said in answer to a question from Judge Orie about missing bones that -- that none of these issues should be treated as criteria but as elements in the assessment that you make. Now, my question is this: When you're coming to the conclusions that you've come to here, are you looking at all of these factors together to build up an impression and a picture based on your experience of having exhumed, you say, more than 400 bodies in this region? In other words, this is an overall assessment rather than any specific individual criteria.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It is an overall assessment based on elements that are the photographs, the autopsy reports, the location where the bodies were recovered, the state of the bodies as described by my colleagues, the bodies as I see them on the photographs. It's a whole series of elements that will lead me to say that this indicates such-and-such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want, if I may, to turn to the question of larvae, because you -- you, I think, have been supplied by the Prosecution, Mr. Dutertre, with some material evidence in a transcript from Mr. Dourel, a forensic entomologist. And just before I give you the opportunity to comment on that evidence, can I just ask you to look at, first of all, body R-1, where we see under question number 2, you have noted for body R-1 the presence of dipterous larvae on the clothing and in the cranial cavity. And then if we -- and you have assessed from the totality that that body had been at the scene for a very short time. If you could then turn to R-9 for a moment. We can see there that you have recorded no larvae or flies and no invading or colonising grass amongst the environmental factors. And you have reached the same conclusion; namely, a very short presence at the location. Could you just help the Trial Chamber understand. In one case, you noted there was a presence of dipterous larvae; in the other case, you noticed an absence of larvae. But having regard to the totality, you concluded in both cases that the body had been present for a very short time. Could you just help the Trial Chamber understand, then, what importance attaches to the presence or absence of larvae in that assessment?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I believe that there is a major difference between R-1 and R-9, and that's -- that is shown in the report. With respect to R-1, we found dipterous larvae on the clothing and on the cranial cavity. This is a data I gathered from the autopsy report prepared by my colleagues. As for R-9, no larvae were described, so I said that no larvae or flies had been described or recorded. Therefore, there is here major difference between the two bodies that led me to come to the same conclusion. When it comes to R-1 and R-9, you will see that both these bodies were found on the ground in the surface and that in the case of one of these bodies, it was covered with a plastic bag over the upper half of the body and there was a jute sack over the legs. Plastic is a material that keeps humidity, that retains humidity; therefore, the body will -- the upper part of the body that is covered with plastic will necessarily be in a -- a higher state of decomposition. And because of humidity, the larvae, the eggs, may develop more rapidly and they can also develop better, because they are very comfortable, in a humid environment, away from light, and they will necessarily develop. Therefore, the difference between those two bodies is that one of the bodies was covered by a plastic bag, R-1. When it comes to R-9, you see the body was found in the open air; it was not covered by a plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So just if I can draw those threads together. The fact that one of these bodies had been recorded as having larvae present in the cranial cavity and on the other body there was no larvae present, that does not affect your conclusion that both of them had been present at the scene for a very short time; is that correct?
