utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a criterion amongst other criteria, but with -- based on the other criteria, I reached the same conclusion. There were dipterous larvae on R-1 because R-1 was in such a state that the dipterous larvae were able to develop more rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, coming to -- to the report of Monsieur Dourel, the forensic entomologist. If I could just very crudely summarise the testimony that he gave to the Tribunal. First of all, he testified - I hope I get the thrust of it right - that it's not possible to pinpoint either a date of death or the length of time a body has been present at a location by reference to the presence or absence of larvae unless you have data about the species and the environmental conditions that have prevailed. Now, that's the first proposition. Now, can I -- can I ask you just to help us as to how you respond to that, given that you have noted the presence or absence of larvae as one of the relevant factors in your overall assessment.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Let me say, first of all, that my comment -- my observation is the same as the observation made by the forensic experts, because they recorded that comment in their reports and I worked on the basis of their reports. I don't know who is Mr. Dourel. I was told there what he had done. But I believe that his technician, a sort of technician has a very short -- narrow perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I am aware that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a technical expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you have a train at 7.30 and you're not available for testimony tomorrow. Could you please focus on the question. The question is -- this is the criticism you're not invited to comment on the qualities of a person you apparently do not know. You are not invited to draw our attention to the fact that your conclusions are the same as the others. You are invited to answer the question. The question is: What your comment is or Mr. Dourel's comment or the main line of his testimony, that if you don't know the details of the atmospheric circumstances and if you don't know what species of larvae there are found, that it -- you're in the situation where you couldn't draw any conclusions from the presence or absence. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To answer this question, I had to tell you that we are not talking about the same level of expert opinion or expertise. The -- the report I prepared with my colleague is a forensic expertise, based on the reports prepared by other forensic experts. I'm not judging in any way the work done by this gentleman, but he's not working on the bodies. He works on technical procedures, on scientific procedures. He does not work in the field. So to come back to what he said, no, I do not agree. The absence or presence of dipterous larvae is significant. We, as forensic experts, are trained to observe these larvae. I believe that the data related to the environment is indeed significant, scientifically speaking. When a body is buried in the ground 50 or 80 centimetres below ground, I believe that you will not find any dipterous larvae. You will only find dipterous larvae on a body as soon as the body -- as the person dies. Diptera flies, diptera are the first insects to appear on the body. Diptera are various kinds of flies. They are 100 and 1.000 [as interpreted] flies, sorts of flies in the world. In Canada, they wrote an article, and there are 7.000 different flies. These flies will lay eggs in the ocular cavity. It will take seven days for the maggot to appear on the body. It's a very small larva, and its length varies, depending on the species of the fly. These maggots turn into pupa, and these pupa - that is to say, the shell of the larvae - the pupa remain on the body or in the clothes. Pupation usually takes place between 10 to 14 days of the death. And the maggot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to focus on the question. The question is -- I think that there's no disagreement on how larvae develop and when they are pupae. The issue is that an expert -- Let me first ask you: Do you know Mr. Dourel? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know his work? Do you know his work, his expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- are you aware of the research he did as he explained it to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of the experience he has gained during his professional life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not. No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless you -- nevertheless, you permit yourself to disqualify him and compare his expertise to yours, which is quite interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the question. Yes, could you please focus on the question put to you by Mr. Emmerson. That is: Do you have any comment to the testimony of Mr. Dourel that if you do not know the details, the data of the circumstances, and if you do not know what species of larvae or diptera are involved, that you couldn't draw any conclusions from either the presence or the absence of these -- these findings -- the presence or the absence of -- of a larvae or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just to make sure that I'm clear. And perhaps I'm mistaken, but since -- I want to make sure I know where we're going, for purposes of determining what examination, if any, I need to make. It was my understanding that the professor just commented with regard to a Canadian article in which there was discussion over a fair number - I think she's mentioned the figure of 7.000 different species of larvae. So I don't know whether or not she was in fact addressing the question that was being put forth by Mr. Emmerson or not. I'm trying to just make sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I got the impression that the witness was not focusing on the answer of Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Guy-Smith, if Mr. Emmerson would disagree, I would expect him to raise his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I -- I appreciate that. But since I -- I'm -- as I've indicated to the Chamber, I'm going to foreclose my examination in order to expedite the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to make sure we can take care of it all at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. Mr. Emmerson, when I again phrased the question, was it a question you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm obviously keen to give the witness an opportunity to comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- both on the a-- of the question but also the relevance and the scope of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't have objected to when Your Honour took issue to the witness, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I would not have any problem in the witness giving her expression on the expertise of another witness and what her experience would be, et cetera, et cetera. But then at least I expect her that know what that experience is what expertise is --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I had understood that the Prosecution had provided Professor Lecomte with Mr. Dourel's materials. And what -- my note of her answer was that he was referring -- she was referring to the fact that he's looking at the matter from a narrower perspective. I think that was the words that she --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that, please try to elicit this in follow-up questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just so that we understand, Monsieur Dourel's report is something I think you've seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he's obviously focusing on forensic entomology.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and only on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you've seen his testimony, I think, in this court, have you? Was that provided to you, a transcript of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I think he accepted for his part that he was looking at only one of the criterion and that your report was based on a much wider range of criterion. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And indeed, when your conclusions were put to him, he did not disagree with them and indicate he was not in a position to challenge them.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just help the Trial Chamber understand, if -- if you can, please, what the range -- what the difference is between the approach that you take, as a forensic pathologist who's conducted exhumations, and the -- what you described as a narrow perspective taken by a technical forensic entomologist.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I'm not going to refer to Mr. Dourel again. Mr. Dourel prepared his report, and that's it. But to answer your question, Mr. Emmerson - and I've said it right from the beginning - I do not agree with the initial proposition you gave me. It's not because you don't know the species of the fly. It's not because you're not aware of the environment that you cannot take the larvae into account. I do not agree with that at all. That's why I was explaining to the Presiding Judge that the perspective of Mr. Dourel is of a purely technical nature. It's much more -- it's much narrower. Any forensic pathologist when observing a body will record whether there are larvae or not or pupa or not. If larvae are recorded, even if you do not know what species of flies it is, you have a larvae, you cannot ignore it. That's why I do not agree with the proposition you gave me at the beginning. I could have answered that way, but I was trying to explain to you that the perspective adopted is completed different. One larva is one larva. An absence of larvae is an absence of larvae. It might mean that the bodies were located elsewhere. I knew the superior of Mr. Dourel, and his superior wrote an article stating that if there aren't any larvae, it means that the larvae -- the body has been displaced, has been transported. I do not agree with Mr. Dourel when he says that because there are -- the fact of -- the absence of presence of larvae has no meaning. It's -- it's one element amongst others that you have to take into account. That's why I made that digression, and I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that explanation. You also said -- you said a moment ago that it's something that forensic pathologists habitually record. And little earlier on -- I think the answer may have got lost in translation a little. A little earlier on, you said that your inclusion of reference to the presence or absence of larvae was something that you took from the forensic pathological reports prepared by the Serbian forensic pathologists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So they -- they -- they plainly considered it a -- a relevant factor to record; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. A forensic pathologist has to record everything he or she observers -- observes. That's a rule, a cardinal rule that's part and parcel of the work of a forensic pathologist. It's a work made of observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can -- on this question of narrow and broad perspective and totality, going back to the distinction that you drew between a criterion for determining date of death or length of presence at the scene and an element in an overall evaluation, can you help us, please, as to whether or not the presence or absence of dipterous larvae was, in your judgement, a sole decisive factor in any one of these cases?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: For me, it's an element amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could just turn very briefly to your conclusions at the conclusion section of your report, please. I want, if I may - just bear with me for one moment - I want, if I may, to look first at paragraph 2 on page 118, which summarises, obviously, information that you have recorded earlier in the report. Paragraph 2 records that "The six bodies, the Re bodies, found around the economic farm are all at the same stage of decomposition, their death being estimated at a relatively recent time, 8 to 15 days, or three weeks for two of them." And just to be clear, you stand by that conclusion, Professor Lecomte?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I wrote it and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come back to the first part of paragraph 3 in -- in a moment or two. Can I ask you, please, just to look at paragraph 3(b) for a moment. And this relates to the remains recorded as having been recovered in the canal itself. You -- if you look at the top of page 119 - 119 - you conclude as follows: "One cannot eliminate the possibility that the bodies which are significantly skeletonised and without dipterous larvae were brought to the canal subsequently and mixed with more recent bodies, their putrefied soft parts having been washed away from inside the clothes by the current." Again, can I ask you, is that a conclusion that you stand by?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Immediately beneath that, you deal, firstly, at (c) with those bodies that were on the surface on the ground adjacent to the canal wall, and you describe them as being very much changed, and you say that their aspect suggests that death occurred more than 3 to -- or between 1 and 2 months before. But overall you say that: "They are frequently incomplete, dislocated, without dipterous larvae, although they were found on the surface of the ground in the open air. The possibility that they were previously buried in the ground and then transported to the site cannot be eliminated". Is that a conclusion you stand by?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And indeed -- and indeed you've told us today that you consider it to be more likely than not that that is the position.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I stand what -- by what I wrote in my report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the bodies - at (d) - buried in the ground, at the bottom of the wall, you say: "Are changed, fragmented, skeletonised, covered in mud." And again, in those case, you express the view that it is not possible to eliminate the possibility of transport to the site. And, again, is that a conclusion that you stand by?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then finally you say this in the bottom part of the conclusions: "Consequently, the circumstances of the deaths cannot be determined, which leaves a large margin of doubt as to the exact place and course of events." And can we assume you stand by that conclusion as well?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to turn back, please, to -- in the conclusions section to paragraph 3(a), where you refer to two bodies that are visible at the level of the overflow, which you say: "Showed signs of immersion of approximately one week." I wonder if you could be handed a blue file of photographs. This is Volume 3 of the Haradinaj forensic cross-examination bundles, the blue file. If you could just turn behind tab 1 for a moment, Professor Lecomte. I know that you've viewed the video itself. This is a still photograph. And, for the record, I'm referring to Exhibit D31. Are these the two bodies that you are there describing?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Upon analysing and reading the documents and getting the documents that I received, I can confirm those are those two bodies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if we can just invite you to look in a little bit more detail, please, at the first of the two. This is behind tab 2, Exhibit D43. Can you see that? I'll just ask you to confirm that that is a photograph that you are focusing on, Professor Lecomte.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: The one that you are showing me is not the photograph that I have in the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In fact there's a discrepancy. I'm sorry. It may be my fault. First of all, I want you to look at tab 2 in the bundle, which is Exhibit D43. And I think what we have on the screen is Exhibit D44. No, I have it the wrong way round. Could we -- could we put up D44 on the screen, please. I'm sorry. It may be my mistake. So let me put the question to you again. Behind tab 2 is a photograph in more detail of one of those two bodies. There we are. And that is Exhibit D44. Now, we've -- and behind tab 3 is a more detailed photograph of the other of those two bodies, which then is Exhibit D43. Now, we've seen -- and I'm -- I know you have seen the video of those two bodies which shows them in more detail. And I don't know whether you recall that the fingers are intact and the toes are intact, as they can be seen on the video.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I believe that I had seen some signs at the level of the hands, but your picture is extremely unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: So I cannot work with this picture. I must have worked either with -- either with a magnifying glass or otherwise in order to look at the hands. The hands are something very important when a body has spent time in the water. The maceration of the skin is a very important element when it comes to forensic analysis. I don't remember if that was the case for these two bodies, but I do remember that on some bodies I had noticed a maceration of the palm of the hands, which was whitish, which meant to me that those people had spent a certain amount of time in the water. And I believe that they had spent approximately one week in the water. I believe that those are those two bodies, but this picture does not actually enable me to say anything precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think you had the videotapes available to you of the crime scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, we have looked at videos, indeed. But I believe that if we put in the conclusion of the report that the body is showing signs of immersion approximately one week long, it must mean that there was maceration, rather the whitish appearance of the skin at the hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think if you look a little earlier in your report, under the heading "Discussion," there are a series of subheadings. And -- and under the subheading "The state of the bodies," you have two tables. And immediately following the second table, you have made a further observation in respect of these two sets of remains. This is -- this is on page 112 of the French version. And I think it's clear, is it not, from that that you were working from the video recordings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you -- you say there: "These bodies of increased volume have preserved their natural skin colour without advanced putrefaction. The hands are discoloured, whitish, and crumpled at the initial phase of maceration, which indicates recent immersion, less than two weeks." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I do maintain what I -- I stand by what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is it possible, looking at those two photographs -- is it possible -- and bearing in mind the video and your findings there, to give an approximate, as approximate as you like, estimation of how long those bodies had been dead?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: The death must have been recent, because the -- the bodies are still swollen and -- and, you know, it's very difficult to know exactly. But what I was able to notice is that I had seen that their natural skin colour was there. But the pictures that you are showing me here are not precise enough. I would not be able to analyse anything from this picture. If I said the bodies were swollen, I mean that they're not -- it's not bones, it's not a skeleton. We're under the impression that those bodies were not put in the water for a long time, that they had not spent too much time in the water. I believe that those bodies had fallen in the water and they are in the water. These are not bodies that were dead for a long time. They must have been dead not long before the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, as I say, it's clear from your report that you were working from the videotape. I don't play it unless anybody asks me to. Could you now turn -- if you look in the bundle a little bit further on, you will find some tabs numbered 18 onwards. And if you could just turn, please, to the tab numbered 21 and 24. That's R-21 and R-24. Now, you will there see the photographs that show the recovery of the upper and lower part of a single body, R-21 and R-24. Do you see those pictures? Do you see those pictures?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I am not able to find it. I cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am absolutely certain that those exhibits are already in the file. Could we have maybe exhibit numbers? Could Mr. Emmerson give us an exhibit number for those two documents. I think that these documents were tendered through Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Emmerson, I think that Mr. Dutertre made a good suggestion that whenever you draw the attention of the witness to any specific document or photograph, that you precisely as possible identify that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have in the index, the records. It may be that what I will need to do, because I think it's quite right to say that since this index was prepared, some of these photographs have been ascribed exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so may I -- may I check the exhibit numbers and read them into the transcript in due course, bearing in mind that we are dealing here with the photographs behind tab 21/24.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Professor Lecomte, in your report, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a constant request that we make. This is not the first time that we make such a request. But I am satisfied with this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Of course it would have been easier if we would have them already available. At the same time, to cause further delays for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to look at two tabs in this bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And once it's done, we will have the exhibit numbers and we'll read them into the record as soon as they're available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, if you could find the relevant passage in your report. You estimated that this body had been dead for approximately two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: What body are you talking about? I'm sorry to ask you. I am slightly lost. There are so many bodies thrown at me in a way that I don't know which body you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 21, which is the same body as 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: R-21 and R-24 are the upper and lower parts of one body and that is the photograph you're looking at in a bundle. Now, you estimated that that body had been dead for approximately two months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I put. I put: "Approximately two months."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, if you would -- just looking at those photographs, please, if you could then turn to the autopsy report. I don't know whether you -- do you read English, Professor Lecomte, or not? Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. If you could -- if you could turn, please, to just a few tabs further back to I, to tab I, which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Madam Usher insist the witness because in the binder at 21 you have certain letters, A, B, et cetera. Mr. Emmerson is now drawing your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I and J, which are --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 1791, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If you could just have a very brief look at that. Behind tab I is the Serbian post mortem report on R-21. And behind tab J is the Serbian post mortem report on R-25, which records the state of decomposition on which you based your assessment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could -- and I'm sorry to do this exercise with you in this way, Professor Lecomte, but can I ask you, please, just to turn back in the bundle to tab number 2, just to remind you of which photograph it is that we're -- which body it is that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I haven't asked you yet. No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No question has yet been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Lecomte. Would you just look --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Behind tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- behind tab 2, where you'll find a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to remind you of that body. Yes? Is it possible that the body behind tab 2 could be the same?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Given the state of decomposition given by my colleagues who made the autopsy, I believe that this is not the same body, because my colleagues - and I noted in the report that I gave you, that I handed you - that those were two decomposed putrefied skeletalised body parts where the soft tissue were absent, there is saponification on the bones and there is no viscera, identifiable viscera. So we're not in the same context here. Maybe you can explain to me what you want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You've absolutely answered the question. I'm not going to ask you to explain it any further. There are reasons why I'm asking you these questions, but I don't need to trouble you with the reasons at the moment. Could you now turn, please, to tab 29, which deals with body R-29. And you dealt with body R-29 in your report at page 69, and indeed you included some of those photographs in the report. So if you could just -- in your report, you concluded, I think, that body R-29 had been dead for more than two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: If this is what I wrote, it means that I had elements to say this is a skeleton. It's dislocated. The soft tissues are putrefied. The body -- the skin is saponified. And I also said that the right hand is detached and that there are bones missing. The fact that bones are missing, I don't know where they are, why they're missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If you could just look through those photographs in the blue file. You've got one at the top there. If you carry on through that tab, you'll see there are some other photographs of these remains. Do you see that? I don't think you have all of the photographs in your report, but you can see the state of the body there, can you?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: There must have been a numbering mistake. They had problems in terms of numbering the bodies. I'm not sure that this is the same body that you're showing me here. If you recall, there had been some mistakes in the numbering of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I think we -- we managed to eliminate the mistakes in relation to this group of bodies. So you can take it that R-29 that appears in that collection of photographs is the same set of remains as you examined the records on. And indeed, if you look at the photograph in your report, you can see, I think, the correspondence between that photograph and the photographs in this bundle. My question to you is -- is a relatively short one. It's the same question I asked you before. But if you have a look at the forensic pathology reports of the Serbian forensic pathologists in relation to R-29, this body is described as having been "in an almost complete state of skeletonisation with no soft tissue, bones bare and dislocated, and all bones found to have been partly connected by ribbons of soft tissue, which were putrefied and dirty grey." Now, is that description, then, consistent with your assessment that this is a body that had been dead for more than two months?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: This particular body does not correspond to this image. This photograph does not at all correspond to this body. This is a body with earth. The other one is in water, which confirms exactly what is said. And I would like to reiterate this, is that the recovery of the body was not made correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not absolutely certain that the witness -- would it be -- would it be -- it would be good if the witness could give us perhaps the numbers, the exact picture numbers that she is looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked the witness precisely on 29a, 29b, et cetera. So in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, first of all, about 29a. Do you see this photograph here as I hold it to you and just make sure you're on the right one. Professor Lecomte, can I just ask you to look towards me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you look at Mr. Emmerson and see what he has --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, you have that photograph, 29a.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if you look at your report, at the second of your photographs in your report for R-29. Do you have -- in your own report, Professor Lecomte, just here.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No, I don't. I do not have the same elements. I worked based on the report of my colleagues on the -- with regard to 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. I think, unhelpfully, we have R-28 on the screen at the moment, which is even further confusing matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to be absolutely clear, Professor Lecomte. If you look at the photographs --

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... There's no question put to you yet at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to take this slowly, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If you look at your report, your own report, you've made some findings in relation to body R-29 on pages 69 and 70. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. This is the problem. I do not understand your question. I am lost with all these numbers and with all these pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Emmerson asked you now - and perhaps you'll look at your screen - is whether it's true that in your report you deal with R-29 at the page you can see on your screen now. That's the only question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, R-29 is the body that is stuck in the branches. And you showed me on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to have the record clear, Mr. Emmerson, I think the witness said that she described R-29 as she finds it on the photograph behind tab 29a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is ERN U003-0042.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. There we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's step one. If you look at page 670 [sic] of your report, you have appended two photographs of body R-29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no page 670. Maybe that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page 70 is what I said. You see the photographs you have in your own report at page 70, Professor Lecomte?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem might be, Mr. Emmerson --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page preceding --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is not page 70. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is page 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- With -- between 69 and 71, isn't it? Because that page, as far as I can see, doesn't bear a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Page -- two -- we have on the screen now page 68. We need to have page 70 on the screen. Just two pages further on, and should look like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- you see now the problem is -- where the numbering is in a bit of an odd place.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, we can see the bottom of those two photographs is -- you've labeled "R 29"; is that right? If you look on the screen in front of you, Professor Lecomte.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes? Now, your conclusion in respect of that collection of remains is that the individual had been dead for more than two months; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I do confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And finally if we could just turn back in the blue file to your left there. If we could turn back to tab number 3. And for the record, I'm referring to D43. Again, I'm just asking you to make the -- the same comparison. This body that we see in that photograph there to your left in tab 2, that can't be the same body, can it?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I wish that this be clearer. This shows you the bad quality of the recovery of the body work. The photographs are re-done, if you wish. Some pictures are not clear. I worked on body R-29. That body had been photographed when it was lifted or recovered on the branches. I worked from the reports of my colleagues regarding R-29. This is what enables me to say this. But I can absolutely not make a -- a correlation between these two. It is impossible. I cannot work like this. I cannot answer this question. This is why I was waiting for your questions. I cannot compare the two bodies. I can absolutely not state anything precisely. This is not a good forensic work. It would not be correct on my part to state anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I am -- let -- let me see if I can just take that one step further with you. A simple question: Looking at the photograph in the bundle of the body that you said had been immersed in water for less than two weeks and that you told us was a recent death. Could that be consistent with the pile of bones that we see in R-29?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following: That we put on the screen now the first photograph, that is, the body in the water; that we then again have the R-29 photograph. Madam Lecomte, you'll be shown two photographs: One of a body in the water, and then another photograph which we discussed before, being R-29. The question after you've seen these bodies, whether there is a possibility that these are identical bodies; that is, at one moment, one day the body in the water, then the next day I take it or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within two days --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Within five days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Within five days that that could have been the body we've seen on the photograph of R-20 -- R-29. So prepare for the comparison of these two pictures and whether this could within a time frame of five days, whether you consider it possible that that would be the same bodies. Could we -- Mr. Emmerson, you have all the numbers. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll start with the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The first photograph is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, it isn't this one. It should be D43.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Maybe if we could just enlarge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And we can, of course, look at the video if need be. But D43 is the first photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged -- could we zoom in a bit more on the body here. That's perhaps too much. That seems to be a ... Could you please look at this body, because you will be asked to compare whether within a time frame of five days this could be the same as the bodily remains we'll see on the second photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the second photograph is 65 ter number 870, page 27. I think that one needs to come out a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that's the second photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, this is the body that you have estimated as being more than two months old. And the question is: Could the photograph that we have just seen turn into that in a space of a few days?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question. I am not trying to avoid answering, but we have clothing here, so we can compare the clothing. So do the clothes that are described by my colleagues on the first picture, do they correspond to this -- to those clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, could you please move on, Mr. Emmerson. I'm also looking at the time. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those are your questions. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will stand by the agreement that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Dutertre, I suggest that we have a break now and that you'll start re-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. But I would like to say that I'm not certain if I will be able to finish within the time that was given to me. I have a lot of questions -- or rather, the cross-examination raised a lot of questions that I -- and I would like to be able to put these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, at the same time, of course, it is a foreseeable result of the Prosecution not presenting the second report of Professor Lecomte. But let's have a break. We'll have a break for 20 minutes, Madam le Professeur. I am aware of your time schedule. We'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Lecomte, I would ask you to respect the break between questions and answers in the interest of the interpreters. Otherwise, it's extremely difficult for people to translate when the Prosecutor and the witness speak the same language. Mr. Dutertre, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Lecomte, on page 42 of today's transcript, you said: "Dogs are not terribly interested in bones." Do I understand you? Is this a problem of translation, or did you indeed say that?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Dogs prefer flesh to bones. When there is flesh, the dogs will rush at it, rather than going for the bones. I mean, the dogs will be attracted to bones only if there is flesh attached to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: What are your exact qualifications in science of canines, foxes, other rodents in general?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I worked at the National Dental Academy in Paris on all types of bites, donkey bites, dog bites, shark bite, rat bites, and we have a significant iconography at the forensic institute, and that is where I've been working for over 20 years now, and I have seen many bodies found in forests, in squats or other areas where there are rats and dogs, where they -- they often gnaw away at their owners to wake them up and they're dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So on the basis of your knowledge, you exclude the fact that a dog might run off with a bone.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: A bone where there's no flesh attached, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: A general question now: Could you describe the limits of an expert assessment of the -- this file.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously any expert report or assessment has limits, whatever they may be. For a file such as this, this particular one, the limits are to do with -- everything to do with the recovery of the bodies. There were no overall photographs taken of the whole site. There were no photos taken systematically, which is whatever we do whenever there is a disaster, whenever there are many bodies, a systematic photo zooming in on the bodies, starting from the broader photograph. That sort of work has not been done. The photographic work was not carried out correctly in situ. And that perhaps explains the discrepancies between certain bodies and so on. And this really has been a major stumbling-block.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you. The photographic documentation and here I'm referring to page 22 of your first report, saying that the video clips don't add any additional forensic element and cannot be used in the context of a forensic study. And my question is as follows: What influence does this have on your report?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Well, on my report, no -- I mean, the work that I had to do to carry out the report, yes, was a considerable influence, because it was necessary to keep looking at, to review and review and categorise and classify things, and it was a huge amount of work and it wasn't made any easier by these video clips. In the video clips, we saw shots of bodies, of VIPs, of people, of trees. The video clips were not carried out as -- as they should have been, as rigorously as they should have been. It wasn't professional work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you didn't have enough in the way of documentation for you to have a full overview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Well, I took the liberty of saying to you that the video clips required a lot of work on our part for us to reconstitute and to work on the report that I then submitted to you. And my second comment is as follows: The -- there is no order in the photographs. They are not technically correct. They're sometimes fuzzy. And they're not the sort of photographs that we would take, where we have the -- the -- starting with a general photograph and then zooming in. Photographs are -- are somewhat random, a body here, a body there, a tree, a spade. I mean, it's really not acceptable work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So that was difficult in your study. It was an obstruction.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It was an obstacle. It made it difficult for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: We have 2076 under 65 ter. It's the aide-memoire that was drawn up. There are two tables. And it was sent last week to Professor Lecomte.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What will be the status of that document, or is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what is the basis of its use -- the legal basis of its use? Because it includes, among other things, opinions made by Mr. Dutertre himself as an advocate. It refers to precisely what he's doing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, what's -- how would you like to use this or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I use it as an aide-memoire, as a paper support to facility everybody's following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For us or for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because it's -- because it's, well, I'd say, to some extent it's leading to conclusions, especially the first part, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I will ask questions, Your Honour, on this part. It's mainly to have the exhibit numbers, references, that sort of thing, and to speed things up, given that I don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Could we -- would there be a possibility the first -- the first table to have the left column only on the screen, which gives us a -- where we find the reference to the report? And then you could ask questions to the witness about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would the Defence agree that is an appropriate way of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm equally concerned about the second table, because as Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let's -- first start with the first table and then see with the second table what to do with that. Please proceed, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor Lecomte, you have two tables that were sent to you last week: A first table that might have possible errors in it. Have you taken -- are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you agree with this document or only with part of it or not at all?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: This document is your document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness answered the question in -- in the way I would expect her to answer this question. Mr. Dutertre, what do you mean by agreeing with the document? That it does exist or it that gives the right references to the report? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the mistakes that are mentioned in the document, Your Honour. But given the answer, I can move straight on to the different mistakes in order to obtain clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We had at the beginning, which is that he's indicating both factual and legal conclusions and testifying and attempting to impeach his own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in a situation at this moment, Mr. Guy-Smith, where Mr. Dutertre called the witness and did not rely on potential evidence because, as he explained to us, he considers it's not up to the standards of what he expects from an expert in this respect and there are too many mistakes. Now, since the Defence has chosen to introduce this evidence, under those circumstances, of course, Mr. Dutertre is not impeaching his witness on any matter he wants to introduce through this witness, but he more or less is in the position that he hardly has any possibility, since that material has been introduced by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I -- I understand the Court's interpretation of Mr. Dutertre's position. But seeing as that he sought to introduce one report by the same expert witness and has found fault with the second report, I don't think that -- that we can actually take that precise position and, rather, he's avoiding conclusions that he doesn't care for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which based upon -- based upon -- based upon the fact, as we know, that the information that he received from another expert, which was limited to a very specific issue, is something that he prefers to the conclusions that this expert has made based upon -- based upon a combination of factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My only issue right now -- my only issue right now is the issue of him alluding to them as errors. Once again, if he wishes to go to the first table and if he wishes to ask questions about the first table, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are some matters which seems to be less traumatic than others. Let's wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, where something was filmed, for example, might be a matter which is not that critical to ... Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed, but we find ourselves in a rather sui generis position to expert reports. You'll be closely followed by the Defence and by the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do appreciate that I will be followed closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Page 107 of your report, sixth line: "35 bodies or fragments of bodies numbered R were found near the Radonjic canal." Is this insertion exact? The professor said that there were a number of markers -- there were a number of markers that have been attributed to clothing, items of clothing. And this is confirmed on pages 24, 52, 63, and 78 of your second report.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: This is not a mistake. This is quite simply numbering that forensic pathologists do when they find something close to a body. It's a sort of numbering, 35, that has brought to 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So it's not 35 bodies or fragments of bodies that have been numbered. There are fewer, because there are certain markers attached to clothing.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Clothing, yes. And there is one where there are some bones. So these are fragments of bodies or -- they're fragments. It's the numbering system. That's how it's numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, let's move on. This seems not to be a very critical issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it goes to show that there are a number of errors that have crept in and they're not insignificant. And I just wanted to draw this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... But just putting the question referring to numbers assigned to clothes. And, of course, the Chamber is aware that sometimes two numbers cover one body. So therefore it's -- does it affect in any way the conclusions? Because that's, of course, the major issue, if we are talking about an expert report. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the question is really to do with accuracy of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Page 4 of your report, you're talking about the numbering, "E," for the economic farm, and you referred to R-5 and R-7 that were close, that they were compared, and they're just from one body.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Actually, it's Re-5 and Re-7. It's a typo, another typing error. But that is part -- to be seen in an overall context in this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Page 113. Page 113, paragraph 4 of -- R-21, R-22, R-23, and R-24. These are the body references. And you say: "R-21, R-22, R-23 -- it's R-21, is it, and not R-20? So it's another typo?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: There are typos all over this report. You have to take the report as a whole and not just take a look at this specific typo. Because obviously it's taken then as part of an overall system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On body R-10, page 33 of the report, it says that the body is visible, it's on the earth with -- it's rocky ground. It's the bottom of a concrete wall. And you say it's in the open air and there's no desiccation. Now, I understand that as the body is in the open air, is one of the elements that you've used to draw your conclusion as to the time -- the -- the length of -- the stay of the body at that place.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Amongst other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like us to see video P452, from minute 24.24 to minute 24.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So this is the situation of body R-10 before it was exhumed. You see it on a pile of rubble. And now I'd like us to see the same video from 51.50 to 1.00.36.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: From 59.50 to 1.00.36.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we'll stop at 1.00. That's marker 10. I don't think anyone would dispute that. That's on the screen. So we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, the body R-10 that we see here, do you think it's visible and in the open air?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: First of all, you showed me a video where there was a pile of rubble. Well, I can accept that it was under the pile of rubble that the body was to be found. Then in the second part to have video that you show me, you can see people raking away the rubble to find a body or to reveal a body covered in the -- in soil underneath this. But let me say one thing: The body has not been buried, because if you're burying, you dig a hole to place the body in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: My question is: Is it visible in the open air?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It's visible. There are bones that you can see. On the photos that I have based myself on, we can see that it's not buried. It's not in the earth. "Visible" is a term that -- well, once again, is perhaps too important for you. I think really it would have been important to point out to the expert that all words count from the point of view of their significance and so on. Now, I would say the body is not buried in the earth. There are stones. There's rubble around. There are many stones. It's at the base of a concrete wall. These are the photos that I used to say it was visible, because you can see the emerging body, and that's what you see on the body -- on the photos that I used. We're not having to use a digger, an excavator to get the bodies out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think so we -- we are at this moment we are discussing whether the body -- whether bone fragments were visible or whether the whole of the body was visible. We've seen the pictures. Some elements of the body were apparently visible. Many others not. That's -- would that ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. There were no parts of the body that were visible. It's rather long -- rather lengthy to show it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the first things I saw on this -- first of all, it's Professor Aleksandric -- the bone fragments that were on the surface of a heap of gravel. And I saw him manipulating what appeared to be a lower jaw and put that at the side. At least, the person in the photograph. But let's -- is it -- how important is it to have a long discussion on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the importance is as follows: If we draw conclusions from the fact that a body was in the open air or wasn't in the open air, in order to determine whether it spent a long period or a short period in situ, then the starting observations have to be precise. R-10 was not -- neither visible nor in the open air. It was under a pile of rubble. And the bones that were visible - that's R-10-1 - and I'll show you that, if necessary, through a series of photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen the photo -- we've seen the video and we've heard the comment by Professor Lecomte. What more to -- to be there? Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do indeed think this is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, you say that the body R-10 is in a ventilated area. Do I understand correctly that this is a criterion that's used in your conclusions as well?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: When a body is not buried or in a confined space - in other words, really buried, some 50 to 80 centimetres below the surface or in a confined space - then it's under stones or rubble. And there's always air that creeps in. There's movement of air inevitably, always. Even if you've got a pile of stones-. So that's a criterion that ... Well, it's not in the open air in the same way as other bodies are. I will agree with you when you say that. There is mud that covers it. But it's not buried. It's on the earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Just a moment. This conclusion that we find in the middle here: "The heap of gravel where R-10 is found is not a ventilated environment." Whose conclusion is that? Is it an expert conclusion or is it your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Aleksandric himself says that the body was buried and that he unearthed it from the pile of rubble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- no, Mr. Dutertre, to get this quite clear, there -- this box is -- or this column says "commentaire." Now, whose comment is it? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are from the OTP, and there are comments on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's another matter. But the middle column, which I consider not to be -- on the screen, are comments by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On the image, you can see a trace of humidity, Professor. Does this prove that this is a ventilated area?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I think that there's a fundamental error here. When you say that the Professor Aleksandric said that he unearthed the body, "unearthed" means that the body had to have been buried under the earth. But you can't unearth somebody from under a pile of rubble. You push away a pile of rubble. You don't unearth. Secondly, there's another important thing, the trace of humidity. Well, I agree that, yes, there is humidity here, and I think that the storms and the heavy rainfall that occurred -- because it's a slope, after all. There was heavy rainfall that came down and brought down rubble, which came up against the wall, which explains the humidity and the -- the body that's next to it. So there's no desiccation of this body, of the clothing, of the body of anything. But really there's something very important I would like to say here. In order to assess and understand all of this, let me come back to what I've already said. You need to take a look at a number of different elements. You can't just take the fact that there's no desiccation. Well, obviously there's no desiccation, because as you say, you were close to -- well, I mean, there's something you can see that's important. You can see barbed wire. Nobody said anything about the barbed wire. Where does that come from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Madam Lecomte, Madam Lecomte. From the -- both language, I do understand that Mr. Dutertre is not in any way seeking further comments on the dessechement du corps but, rather, on the ventilation. Let's move on, Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. R-14 and R-15 now, Your Honour. On pages 41 and 43 of the report. So R-14, R-15, pages 41, et seq.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: For R-14, "absence of dipterous larvae, the body is above ground in the open air." And for R-15, "the body was found on the earth next to rocks." Now, I understand that the fact that the body is in the open air is an element that makes it possible for you to draw your conclusions as to the length of stay of that body at that particular site.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: And I've said - and I'll say it again - that saying that there's a very short stay. To do that, we draw on a number of arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But that's one of the criteria that you used.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It's one of the elements, not criteria. Let me say that when a body is not buried, if it's not buried in a confined space, it is ventilated, even though there are stones around. And if you take a look at the photos that I used on my work - these are the photos that you have on page 42 - you can see that we can see the body parts. In fact, it's numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Thank you. And I'll come back to those photos. Dr. Aleksandric's report, Exhibit 412, page 3 - but I'll quote it to you - states: "[In English] About 2 metres to the right of the body labelled R-10, that is to say, at the end of the outside edge of the concrete wall -- outside edge of the concrete wall, there was a pile of gravel. There were no human bone fragments on or around it. However, since there was projectile damage on the wall overlooking the pile of gravel, it was suspected that there might be a body underneath the pile of gravel. Once it had been removed, two more bodies were discovered and subsequently labelled R-14 and R-15." [Interpretation] I'd like to show the video P452, 08.15 to 08.19, which shows you the pile of gravel at issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would seem there's a technical problem here. Well, let's go to 36.02 to 36.49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can see people who are digging into this pile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would ask Mr. Dutertre to not comment on what we are seeing. We can all see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop here. And now I'd like to move on to a further -- another video clip, 65 ter 2074 from 7.26 to 8 minutes 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could start at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop here at 7.50. We've seen enough. I'd like an exhibit number for this video, Your Honour, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection. Then it's admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, bodies R-14 and R-15, do they look like bodies that are in the open air, as is stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Let me come back to two points. First of all, this footage is just a video clip and just that. The report of the professor you've mentioned - I don't remember his name - has as much value as my own report. I repeat that we are here to help the judicial system. We are not prosecutors here. I'd like to say that all the things that are removed with shovels here are rubbles, are stones. The body was not underground. The body was not buried. And we can see that they remove this rubble to the other side. You can interpret any photograph any which way. Personally, I prefer to base myself on general observations. I don't think you can make any final conclusions based on documents that are not detailed enough. These bodies are above the ground but under a heap of gravel. It's not cement, and the air -- it was very possible for the air to reach the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, the Chamber is not assisted by an ongoing further debate on whether a body under a heap of pebbles, where we do not know to what extent it allows further ventilation or not, or whether that's a body covered by or in the earth or upon the earth but covered by -- that's -- all these examples now have shown that Professor Lecomte considered that if a body is not, I would say, solidly embedded in the earth itself but if it's -- even if it's covered by quite a lot of things that she considers, that this is not in the ground but on the ground and that ventilation is still possible. We are not much assisted by -- I don't know what -- what else there to come, but these are almost semantic discussions, rather than anything else. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it goes beyond a semantic discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let me proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: When it comes to entomological matters, do I understand well that you've used the entomological data as one of the elements allowing you to draw your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Do you have a university background as an entomologist?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No, but I am a trained pathologist and a pathologist is supposed to -- I'm a trained forensic pathologist, which is general training. We work on toxicology, on all the domains covering forensic pathology. We also study soil, bites, everything, and also vermin, because we are supposed to describe the vermin we find. We are not supposed to interpret it, but we are supposed to describe what we find.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, you were on your feet. I did not immediately respond --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there were a couple comments I was going to make, with regard to the last question asked by Mr. Dutertre. First of all, once again, it seems that we -- that he is intending to impeach his own witness. Second of all, we have seen a number of experts. Individuals have been called by the Prosecution for their expertise who have commented on a myriad of fields. With regard to the issue of pathology, I believe it's been recognised by the Chamber that a pathologist takes into account multiple disciplines in order to make a determination of their ultimate conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record. Mr. Dutertre, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Mr. Dourel told us that in the institute he works for, people spend one year training to identify various species of flies or larvae. What sort of training do you have in terms of identifying -- larvae identification?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: No, we can't go on like this. I can't go on like this, because at the ICRG, where -- the institute you're referring to, I've told you that they study the development of a larvae in a jar. They conduct research. They bury sheep and unearth them and so on and so forth. But that's not what I do. I am a forensic pathologist, and my colleagues, my Serbian forensic colleagues made a number of observations. I'm saying that dipterous larvae is different from coleopterous larvae. In one case you have little legs. The coleoptera has little legs and it comes third. The dipterous larvae is a maggot. It's a fly. And of course I've got some training in that matter. Of course it's not the type of training you would like me to have, but I've got the same type of training as any other forensic pathologist in the world, the basic training that allows me to make the difference, the distinction between the coleoptera larva and the dipterous larva. I'm not -- I'm not blaming you in any way. I'm just trying to get things quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Would you agree that Mr. Dourel has a higher degree of specialisation when it comes to entomology?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know him. I knew his former superior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see what it has to do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, we're not inviting this witness to comment on the level of expertise of another witness. It may be clear that if you're a general practitioner that you might have quite some knowledge of the functioning of the heart but perhaps not as much as a cardiologist. So therefore that's understood. It's clear from the testimony of Mr. Dourel that -- that he focused and spent more time on these issues than a general medical pathologist would do. That's clear for the Chamber. It -- I don't think that this question and -- and the answer would -- would essentially contribute to the understanding of this issue by the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seem to understand that you do not share the views of Mr. Dourel. You do not agree with his conclusions. Let me take a number of examples. When you talk about R-1, R-2, and R-4 in your report, you mention that diptera are present. So the presence of diptera is one of the elements you've used to draw your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It's one of the elements I've used amongst other elements. I would like to stress one thing: I believe that I'm being -- I'm being put on trial here. My colleague is working on larvae. My job is to work on the -- to describe the appearance of a larva. I'm not going to go into too much detail about that. We do not have the same field of expertise. His perspective is much narrower. He's a specialist, a technician, a fly technician, if I may say so. I'm not in the same time in the same line of work, so I can't say anything about what he said. My Serb colleagues who prepared the autopsy reports also recorded the larva -- the dipterous larvae. They mentioned that there were maggots and nothing more. I don't see what it adds to the report. They just mentioned that there were dipterous larvae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Lecomte, don't feel attacked. At least, it's not the Chamber's wish that anyone here is attacked. Which doesn't mean that the testimony of a witness or an expert could not be tested. I think that Mr. Dutertre is trying in his way to test your testimony. And could you please focus on the questions specifically put to you. Mr. Dutertre, you know there's a saying that -- about specialisms that specialising means knowing more about less until finally you'd know everything about nothing. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less and less about -- more and more about less and less. Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: In their reports, your Serb colleagues do not use the expression of "dipterous larvae." At page 6594 [as interpreted] of the transcript, Mr. Dourel states that: "The conclusions in the autopsy report related to R-1 do not allow the conclusion that these are dipterous larvae." He also says that there are coleopterous larvae that -- and it's very difficult to differentiate them from dipterous larvae with the naked eye. The same applies to R-2 and R-4. Since you did not have any larvae samples at your disposal and since the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I read on the record page 6594. Checking the testimony of Mr. Dourel, I'm in the 8.000s, rather than -- or am I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 8594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
