utterances.text: You did not have any larvae samples at your disposal and the conclusions of the Serbian forensic specialists regarding R-1, R-2, R-4 are very limited. Can you be very sure that we are talking about dipterous larvae or coleopterous larvae?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I'm going to try to stay very calm, but the dipterous larvae is the most frequent larvae, the most -- that occurs the most frequently on a body, because it's a fly. Whether the coleoptera is a sort of beetle. It does not arrive on the body immediately. The fly comes immediately on the body, lays an egg that produces a larva. A coleoptera is a type of beetle that has little flies. It will come -- arrive later on the body and the larva is different. I cannot say whether it was a coleopterous larvae or a dipterous larvae, but considering that you have flies everywhere, on pieces of cheese or whatever, flies produce dipterous larvae. That's it. But I did not go beyond that. I did not go and see whether -- what type of insects they were dealing with. I did not have the necessary data. And the technician you ask, you -- you referred to is right when he says that you can't tell the difference. I'm saying that in 99.9 of the cases the first on the body are flies and not coleopteras.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: So you can't say with absolutely certainty that it's dipterous larvae and not coleopterous larvae?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I'm saying it's a certainty of 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On body R-3 -- or should I understand that the absence of flies or dipterous larvae is also an element that may enable you to make your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: These are not official conclusions. I believe that I sent you the report. I thought that you read my report. I said it tells us -- it tells us -- it indicates, indicates. So I answered earlier that it's an ensemble of elements and it is the practice of exhumed bodies enable us to say that it indicates something. This is not a strict argument. It's not a definite argument, a formal argument like that grass is not a formal argument. But this is what is seen most often in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dourel, on page 8595 and 8596 of the transcript stated that at a certain point in time the larvae go on to immigrate on to -- to burrow down into the ground and in order to make-- to take samples, you have to take samples of the soil. And if the samples are not available, it is impossible to exclude that a body without any larvae that was not colonised by the larvae, where it is found by larvae that had immigrated down into the soil, that had migrated down into the soil, rather. And you are describing R-3 as a body that had a very advanced state of skeletonisation, page 18 in French. The expert Mr. Dourel explained to us at page 8565 - 8605, rather - 8605 of the transcript that a skeletonised body without any soft tissues is a body that is no longer attractive for flesh-eating insects. Can you -- you are confirming to us that there were no soil samples for body R-3.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I will not answer this question, because I do not agree. For two reasons: First of all, flies go close to the body. If there is a skeletised body, which is the case of this body, we must not forget that the body had clothes totally impregnated of putrid matters and this attracts flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: You did not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Your question is way too long. You have to ask short questions so that I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What type of questions Mr. Dutertre should put is finally for me and for the Chamber to decide. Nevertheless, the suggestion made by Madam le Professeur is a good one, that instead of summarising something -- and your question actually, Mr. Dutertre, you are explaining why you are putting your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question finally just was whether there were any ground samples taken and available to Madam Lecomte. And I think she then, of course, commented on the introduction to the question rather than answering the question. Do I understand you well, Madam Lecomte that, no ground samples were available to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. But I may say something that is very important, if I may. This is really very important. The collection of the soil sample is not necessarily in order to know whether there were larvae. The larvae, when they go on to a body, they -- they land on the clothes that had putrid elements and they lay eggs inside the clothes and then the larvae, they migrate in order to go to the darkness, 2 or 3 centimetres into the soil. So 2 or 3 centimetres of a sample is very easily taken, when it is a sample of 2 or 3 centimetres below the earth. Every word of his report are as important as my every word, so I cannot say or give any -- or give comments that are so general. I do not agree with this procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Lecomte, I wanted to demonstrate that it was just a question about a fact, nothing else, at that moment. But, of course, your expertise, of course the Chamber will finally determine whose expertise assists in making the final determinations the Chamber will have to make. Mr. Dutertre, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Since there were no samples taken from the soil, could you therefore exclude absolutely that R-3 was not colonised prior to the place where it was found?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I cannot answer such a question. First of all, because you should have asked the professor that was on site if he had made some -- taken some samples. I don't know what he did. And second of all, it doesn't mean that because there were no samples taken, that there were no larvae, because there can be some traces of pupa. The pupa is the envelope of the larvae before they go away. And they are positioned, placed on clothes or on body parts. So if they are not described, it means that there are none. But the samples are -- taking the samples or not taking the samples is not a problem. The forensic expert -- you know, we work in two different fields. You should have asked your expert to come and see us, to come and see us, to work with us, because then we would have known. This is two very distinct fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: On page 8618 of the transcript, Mr. Dourel states that the absence -- the visible absence of larvae does not mean that there are no diptera larvae. He said that some maggots can exist, they are very small, that belong to the calliphoridae family, reputed to come to -- onto the body during the last phases of decomposition or putrefaction and that they are very small in size. Is this an element that you took into account when you carried out your expertise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, let's try to -- to separate matters very clearly. From what I understand, from the testimony of this witness, she has seen photographs and a video and has seen reports but has not personally observed the situation. Now, whether this expert has considered the possibility that larvae that were not seen by others and not reported were there is, of course, a very difficult question. It means that whether she took into account - and I didn't get that impression from her testimony until now - whether she took into account the possibility that the experts who were at the site may have overlooked something -- because let's -- let's try to -- to -- to clearly understand what the situation is. If no larvae are reported -- there are two possibilities: Either they were there or they were not reported; or they were not there. That's the situation. How could possibly this expert give any comment on that? If we would ask the expert: Have you also drawn conclusions on possible errors made by the experts who were on site, then I think we would easily fall into speculation rather than in clarifying issues of fact. Please proceed and formulate your questions very precisely in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try, Mr. President, but I will go on to another subject because of our time constraint, but I do not think that I'll be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Anyway, regarding the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear concerning what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have always -- I studied for 12 years. I'm not a botanical expert. You asked me the question. I will ask my colleague. A third report to work with other experts, the experts in the field of larvae, flies, and experts on the agronomy. I am very sad that you did not ask me to bring a third report. You are asking me to give my opinion on a report that I looked at very briefly. I believe that that report was not sufficiently close to reality in order to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Lecomte, I invited Mr. Dutertre to carefully and precisely formulate his question. However, you started already answering a question which was not yet put to you. So Mr. Dutertre is again invited to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that was not entered in the transcript was to know whether you or Dr. Vorhauer had a university degree in plant studies.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: I will repeat. I studied for 12 years, and when it comes to a forensic pathologist, every forensic pathologist must work with other fields and connected fields, and I insist to work with other people, with other experts who are very, very precise, specific. I don't know if you answered -- hear me. We always have to work with other experts. Every time I carry out an expertise, I always call upon another expert on another topic; rather, on -- an expert in the matters of cardiology or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: But I really insist on saying this: You cannot attack me on saying that I don't have diplomas on this or that, on flies or whatever. I have to say that as a good expert witness, I have to surround myself with other experts and we work together as a team. This is the work of a good expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not an attack on you. It is a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't consider it like that. But it is a way -- a technical way -- and we -- unfortunately, we are lawyers. It's a technical way of establishing what education --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you had and what education someone has not had. Let's not enter into a debate, also because I know your traveling schedule. At least --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you feel attacked -- but Mr. Dutertre will now show that he's not attacking you. He's asking questions to you. Mr. Dutertre, proceed -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Lecomte -- at the end --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of your testimony, I'll give you an opportunity to make the comment you'd like to make at this moment. We are under some time restraints. You'll get an opportunity for that. Mr. Dutertre will now put the next question to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like to play a video that already received an exhibit number. It's Exhibit Number V00748 from minute 5 to minute 5.11. I do not have the exhibit number any more, but I -- I think that you found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I hope you can find it as well, the exhibit number. Please proceed. And let's play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, maybe we should play it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can stop here at 5.10, 5 minutes, 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Professor, would you say that when it comes to this slope, there's a lot of vegetation -- not a lot of vegetation, that it's completely depleted of vegetation?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: The image that I have in front of me, it is not a very clear image; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It's fuzzy, no? Don't you agree with me that it's fuzzy?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Well, the quality is not absolutely fabulous, but can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer, because I see some green. I see the green colour, but for me it's a fuzzy picture and I'm not able to interpret it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I understand the answer of the witness to be that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... due to the quality of the images that she's not in a position to give a specific answer on the level of vegetation on this slope. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P400, page 12, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: With the microphone, please, Mr. Dutertre. Could the question be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I didn't have the microphone on. I'd like to have a close-up of photo 60, which is the bottom right-hand photo. My mistake. Actually, it was number 57 that I should have said. That's at the top, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: This photo is better in terms of quality, and my question is as follows: When you take a look at this photo, do you think that the soil surface is equal to, greater than, less than the green area covered in vegetation?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Before I answer this question precisely, I'd like to make a comment. I'd like to know whether the photo was taken once the bodies had been removed and the -- there had been footsteps or people moving around who had turned up the earth while they were recovering the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could zoom in. But I think you'll see very clearly at the bottom of the slope and next to the wall that there are still bodies. So it's before exhumation.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about all of the bodies,.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: Because I'm not entirely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: Yes, you can see some of them at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DOMINIQUE LECOMTE
utterances.text: You don't see all of them. And I believe that there were more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you -- you read our minds. At the same time, you are not here to read our minds but to answer the questions. Certainly one of the next questions would be: When was this photograph taken? Which, of course, is important for the relevance of this question. Nevertheless, I'd like to invite you to answer the questions, but no questions any more at this moment, because we are close to 7.00, and I know that you have to leave. Now, Mr. Dutertre, I take it that you have not yet finished your examination, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is indeed the case, Your Honour. But that would mean that we might have to re-call Professor Lecomte.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll see whether I can come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're asking permission to have Professor Lecomte to be re-called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to know whether Professor Lecomte would -- could come tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will decide whether or not to -- an opportunity will be given to you, Mr. Dutertre, to re-call Professor Lecomte. Of course, we will first try to find out whether Professor Lecomte is available. I take it that the Defence would be in favour to re-call Professor Lecomte in order to put further questions to her, because the order of the testimony is a bit confused by now, to say the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely neutral on the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As am I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm like Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dutertre, that means that the Chamber will consider whether or not you will get an opportunity to re-call the witness for further re-examination. It might also depend on whether the Chamber would have any further questions. At this moment, Madam Lecomte, whatever the Chamber will decide, whenever you'd like to be re-called, I know that you would like to go. Mr. Dutertre, one second only because --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could Professor Lecomte come back tomorrow? Does she have commitments elsewhere that might be postponed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We were informed that Professor Lecomte could not come tomorrow and that she has travel arrangements for today, so therefore it would be at a later stage. That's our information. If it's wrong, Professor Lecomte, please tell us. Professor Lecomte, I'd like to -- I'd like to instruct you that since there is a possibility that you would be re-called for further examination, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony nor the testimony already given or the testimony perhaps still to be given. This is my instruction. If finally the decision will be that you will not be re-called, you'd be informed about that, and then, of course, you're free to speak again with whomever you want about your testimony. Madam Usher, could you please escort Madam Lecomte out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would also -- we would also include in our considerations that I promised you to have an opportunity make any final comments. It might be, if that would be the only reason for us to re-call you, that you'll be invited to put that on paper and send it to us, because -- just to give a comment of the -- I'll let you go now. I know that you're in a hurry. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what the Chamber is anticipating for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've just double-checked my e-mail. I have not received a response from the Prosecution with regard to the issue. They said they were going to file between 5.00 and 6.00. I don't know whether the document is forthcoming or not. I'd like to know where we stand on this issue so we're in a position to address it intelligently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked my staff to inform me immediately, and we have not received anything. At least -- perhaps the staff, but not yet sent to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You won't have received it because it's not finalised, but it will be very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How do you wish to -- I mean, how do you wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to discuss that with my -- my colleagues at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I can't give you any answer to that. Both of you of the last day, and also in view of other matters -- I mean, of course, the Chamber is 24 hours available a day, but -- but sometimes not all 24 hours. We'll see how to proceed, and we'll -- we'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust that we're not meeting at 4.00, 5.00, 6.00, or 7.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, I would not dare to force you to come at this time. There will be communications tomorrow, I take it, how to proceed. Mr. Dutertre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Procedural point: There's the Dourel report that hasn't received an exhibit number yet. And I wonder whether it can be numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. We will ... the Dourel report has not received a number yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar will assign a number to it, but we'll adjourn now. Oh, Mr. Registrar, it's just the one word and ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that, will be P930.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any objection against the Dourel report? I see nodding "no" three times, that means that P930 is admitted into evidence. With the apologies to technicians and interpreters and others who are assisting us, we'll adjourn until tomorrow, same courtroom, quarter past 2.00.
